opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it slightly differently. The point isn't really free time on its own. It's what free time does to the economics of protest, and what that means for how states have historically related to their citizens.

Right now, civil disobedience is self-limiting. If you want to block a road, occupy a building, or flood a city council meeting, you pay a real cost: lost wages, maybe your job, childcare to arrange. Most people can only do it occasionally. So the state can absorb it. It can wait people out, arrest a few, and count on everyone eventually going back to work.

Now imagine a world where a large fraction of people don't need to work, because machines produce most of the value and people live on some kind of transfer. Suddenly the opportunity cost of protest drops to almost zero. You could have millions of people who could, in principle, sit in the street indefinitely. Mechanisms that rely on attrition, like slow-walking a response or arresting ringleaders, stop working when there's no attrition. And our legal system assumes a fairly low base rate of lawbreaking. Courts and police can't process a large share of the population deciding at once not to comply. So in a narrow sense, mass disobedience could become very hard to manage through the usual tools.

But I think the more important and worrying part is what the state does in response. If your citizens aren't economically necessary, because they're not producing tax revenue and not needed as workers or soldiers, then the deep reason states have tolerated dissent and conceded to it starts to erode. Historically, governments gave ground to protest partly because they needed those people to keep showing up. Take that away, and a highly disruptive population with lots of free time looks less like a constituency to bargain with and more like a management problem.

So my worry is that "untenable" cuts both ways. The old equilibrium, where some disobedience is tolerated because it's bounded and because the state depends on the people doing it, breaks down. What replaces it could be much more permissive, but I suspect the more natural pressure is toward heavier surveillance, automated enforcement, and quietly narrowing the channels through which ordinary people can push back. That's part of what I mean by gradual disempowerment. No one has to decide to strip people of power. The incentives that used to protect their voice just stop being load-bearing.

r001.rationale: The candidate says protest costs people wages, jobs, and childcare arrangements, which limits how often they can sustain civil disobedience.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the framing in the question is actually a bit backwards from how I'd put it. The worry I have isn't that civil disobedience becomes untenable for the state — it's that it becomes untenable for the people.

So think about how civil disobedience actually works today. The reason a general strike, or mass protests, or people refusing to show up to work has any teeth is that the state and the economy actually need those people. If the factory workers walk out, the factory stops. If the truckers stop driving, the shelves go empty. If enough soldiers refuse to fire on the crowd, the regime falls. Almost every historical example of ordinary people successfully pushing back against a government runs through this channel: the government depends on your labour, your taxes, your willingness to cooperate, and you can withhold it.

Now imagine a world where, for whatever reason, most people have abundant free time because their labour isn't needed anymore. Maybe AI and robotics are doing most of the economically useful work. On the surface that sounds great — everyone gets to garden and write poetry. But look at what happens to the leverage. If you go on strike, nothing stops. If you refuse to cooperate, the state doesn't lose anything it needed. The threat underlying civil disobedience was always "we'll stop doing the thing you depend on," and if they don't depend on you, the threat is empty.

So it's not that the state can't tolerate disobedience. It's that disobedience stops being costly for the state, which means it stops being a form of power. You'd still be allowed to protest, in some sense — it's just that nobody has to listen.

And I think this is the thing people miss when they say "well, we'll just give everyone a UBI and it'll be fine." Even in the nice version where everyone is materially comfortable, you've shifted from a world where ordinary people hold some structural bargaining power to one where they're essentially being provided for at the discretion of whoever controls the productive capacity — the AI systems, the capital, the state. That could be benevolent for a long time. But it's a very different equilibrium, and historically, groups that have no leverage and are living on someone else's goodwill don't tend to do well over the long run.

So the free time is almost a symptom. The underlying thing is that people have become economically and militarily irrelevant, and civil disobedience is one of the first things to quietly lose its force when that happens.

r001.rationale: The response says people can withhold labor to pressure the state, but does not identify jobs or other responsibilities as practical constraints on how much sustained civil disobedience people can undertake.

astra-6.text:
Well, a lot of the state’s ability to wait out a protest depends on people eventually having to go back to work. You might care deeply about an issue, but you still have rent to pay, and you can’t spend every day blocking a road or occupying a building.

If a large fraction of the population could afford to keep doing that indefinitely, then that changes the balance of power. The state has a limited number of police, limited court capacity, limited prison capacity. It can deal with a small group of people refusing to cooperate. It’s much harder when that’s a substantial fraction of the population and they don’t get worn down economically.

So I don’t mean that free time automatically produces a successful political movement. You still need motivation and coordination. But it removes a major constraint on sustained civil disobedience, and makes simply waiting for people to go home a much less effective response.

r001.rationale: The response says protesters may have to return to work and pay rent, limiting how long they can sustain civil disobedience.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic intuition is that the state has a limited capacity to deal with people who refuse to cooperate. And right now, participating in civil disobedience is expensive for most people. You have to take time off work, you might lose your job, you have rent to pay. So even if you care a lot about an issue, there’s a pretty hard limit on how much time you can spend protesting or getting arrested.

If a large fraction of the population didn’t have those constraints, then sustained noncooperation would become much easier. People could keep showing up. And arresting people, processing them, putting them on trial—all of that takes resources. You don’t need everyone to participate before that capacity starts to get overwhelmed.

But free time alone wouldn’t be enough. People would still need something they cared about, and they’d need to coordinate. So I wouldn’t say it automatically makes the state powerless. It changes the balance by making sustained participation much less costly.

r001.rationale: The response says work obligations, possible job loss, and rent make civil disobedience costly and limit how much time people can sustain it.
